name: Valeeswarar Temple, Kuranganilmuttam
deity: Shiva as Valeeswarar, with the goddess Irayarvalai Ammai (Erayaar Valayammai)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Thondai country, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); a Pallava-era rock-cut cave temple with later additions
dynasty: Pallava (the cave is attributed to Mahendravarman I), with later Tamil patrons
summary: Valeeswarar at Kuranganilmuttam is a small rock-cut Shiva shrine south of Kanchipuram, the Tirukkuranganilmuttam of the Tevaram, whose unusual name is read from a legend of the Lord worshipped by a monkey, a squirrel and a crow.

sections.history: Kuranganilmuttam lies in the old Thondai country south of Kanchipuram, in the valley of the Palar, among the villages that gather near Mamandur. In the Tevaram the place is named Tirukkuranganilmuttam and counted among the shrines sung by the saints, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam; tradition attaches its hymn to the child-saint Sambandar. The sanctum is a rock-cut cave of the Pallava age, and local accounts attribute its excavation to the great builder-king Mahendravarman I, though researchers note that no Pallava inscription has yet been found in the temple or the village to settle the point. Later inscriptions of the Rashtrakuta and Chola periods name the village, and the Lord here is honoured as a swayambhu linga, one held to have risen of its own accord. Through these centuries the little shrine has remained in quiet worship.
sections.architecture: The temple is modest in scale, its heart a rock-cut sanctum in the Pallava manner rather than a towering stone complex. Within, Valeeswarar is worshipped as a swayambhu linga, and the goddess Irayarvalai Ammai is honoured in her own shrine. The cave and its surrounds are remembered for the carved scenes of the beings who are said to have worshipped here in animal form, from which the temple takes its name, and the plainness of the early Pallava rock-work gives the place an austere, archaic character distinct from the great gopuram-crowned temples of the plains. Specific measurements and later structural additions are not well documented in available sources.
sections.legends: The name Kuranganilmuttam is read from its presiding legend. Kurangu is the monkey, anil the squirrel, and muttam the crow, and tradition holds that the Lord was worshipped at once by three devotees in these forms: Vali, the monkey-king of the Ramayana, is said to have prayed here to be freed of his animal shape; Indra is remembered as worshipping in the form of a squirrel; and Yama, the lord of death, in the form of a crow. From the three the village and shrine are said to take their name. Some accounts add Hanuman among the worshippers, and other versions of the sthala-purana differ in detail. These are devotional traditions carried by the temple rather than historical record.
sections.festivals: As a living Shiva shrine the temple keeps Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham, the hours sacred to Shiva, and the ordinary round of the Tamil ritual calendar. Detailed festival schedules for this small rural temple are not well recorded in available sources, so visitors are best advised to enquire locally, especially for any annual festival and for car or procession days, which follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Kuranganilmuttam offers the stillness of a very old and little-visited shrine rather than the bustle of a great temple town. The rock-cut sanctum, the self-manifest linga of Valeeswarar, the goddess in her shrine, and the carved memory of the animal devotees reward an unhurried, reverent visit. The setting is rural, in the Palar valley among fields south of Kanchipuram, and those drawn to the Pallava rock-cut heritage and to the quieter Tevaram shrines will find the place rewarding; it is not geared to large crowds, so patience and local guidance help.

visit.timings: Small rural temples of this kind are typically open for a few hours in the morning and again in the evening, with a long midday closure; timings are not firmly documented, so confirm locally before travelling.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer areas but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals, carvings, or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Kuranganilmuttam is a village in the Palar valley south of Kanchipuram, near Mamandur, reached via Thoosi (Dusi). Kanchipuram, about 10–12 km away, is the nearest large town and transport hub, with rail and bus connections; the nearest major airport is Chennai. Local buses and road transport serve the area, but as a small village shrine it is best reached by private vehicle with local directions.
